# Question 9: Wiring a "Notify on Change" Feature onto an Existing Periodic Job

## Round 1 -- System Design (45-60 min, no code)

### Setup

You have a periodic job that's already in production: on a fixed schedule
(say, every 15 minutes), it fetches a full dataset from an upstream source
and writes it into your database. This job has been running reliably for a
long time. Its one job is to keep that dataset fresh, and nothing else
depends on it doing anything more than that.

Product wants a new feature built on top of it: let users **subscribe** to
individual entities in that dataset, and **email them** when some condition
about an entity they're watching becomes newly true -- a status flips from
"unavailable" to "available," a value crosses a threshold, whatever fits
the domain. The condition can flip back and forth over time (available →
unavailable → available again), and each entity can have many subscribers.

### The prompt

Design the "notify subscribed users when X becomes newly true" feature.
Cover, at minimum:

1. **Where does the detection logic live?** Inside the existing periodic
   job, in a separate process that runs on its own schedule, behind a
   pub/sub or event stream, or driven off a database change-feed? Walk
   through what you'd actually pick and why.
2. **How do you guarantee no missed notifications and no duplicate
   notifications?** The existing job's schedule can overlap with itself
   (a slow run hasn't finished before the next one is due to start), and
   whatever you build has to survive that without double-emailing anyone
   or silently skipping a transition.
3. **What happens when the side-effecting action (sending an email) fails?**
   Retry? Drop it? Queue it for later? Who finds out?
4. **Failure isolation.** If the notification/email path has a bug or an
   outage, should that have any ability to degrade or break the existing
   job's core responsibility (keeping the dataset fresh)? What does your
   design do to enforce the answer?
5. **Secrets.** The feature needs credentials for an external system (SMTP,
   a push provider, whatever). Briefly note how those credentials should be
   handled differently from the rest of your config.

There is more than one reasonable architecture here, and real production
systems have shipped more than one of the options in question 1. You will
not be told upfront which one, if any, matches what was actually built for
the system this question is based on -- you're being evaluated on the
reasoning and the tradeoffs you surface, not on guessing an answer.

---

## Round 2 -- Implementation (3-4 hours)

Open the `impl/` folder next to this file. It's a small, self-contained
TypeScript project (own `package.json`, not part of any larger monorepo)
modeling a stripped-down version of the Round 1 scenario: a sequence of
periodic-job "snapshots" of entities with an open/full-style status, a
subscriptions fixture, and a `processEnrollmentUpdate` function -- the
transition-detection-and-notify logic -- that is currently **unimplemented**
(a stub that throws).

Read `impl/README.md` for exact setup (`npm install`, `npm test`) and
the task. In short: `src/notifications.ts` documents the contract
`processEnrollmentUpdate` must satisfy in a JSDoc comment above the stub;
implement it (and anything it depends on) so the full test suite passes,
without editing the tests or the fixtures. Base your implementation on
your own Round 1 design -- or a revised one, now that you're looking at
the concrete types, fixtures, and mock mailer instead of a whiteboard
sketch.

**Keep a log of the prompts you give to AI tools during this exercise** (a
running text file, a chat export, or equivalent) -- you'll walk through it
in the review. This isn't a test of whether you used AI; it's a test of
how you directed it, what you checked, and what you changed.
